title: The Circle of Power: Something Good for the Last Five Minutes of Class
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart describes a simple closing routine, the "Circle of Power," that he built in response to his principal's push for bell-to-bell learning balanced with what he calls "gentle urgency." Noticing that his students had grown especially distracted and eager to pack up in the final minutes of class, he designed a scripted three-minute closing sequence: students form a standing circle, share something they're thankful for, and the teacher closes by naming something they're grateful for that ties back to that day's learning. The piece is a practical example of turning a chaotic, wasted portion of class time into a structured routine that reinforces both classroom community and Credibility signaling. It's presented as a seasonal, adaptable experiment rather than a permanent fixture.
points: Names the "gentle urgency" balance - honoring school time as a sacred trust while still treating students as whole souls, not desk-bound grinders - as the philosophy behind the routine.
Provides an exact, minute-by-minute script (three minutes: form circle; two minutes: share gratitudes; bell: teacher shares a content-linked gratitude) that other teachers can lift directly.
Targets a specific pain point - increasingly distracted, pack-up-early students in the final minutes of class - with a low-prep structural fix rather than a discipline response.
Doubles as a classroom-community builder and a Credibility signal, folding the same five minutes into content review by tying the teacher's closing gratitude back to the day's learning.
quotes: Instead, he strikes what I call the gentle urgency balance, which I think is key for signaling Credibility to students.
Urgent: on the one hand, school time is a sacred trust, and that trust isn't being honored when students mill around aimlessly for minutes on either end of a class period.

All right, students, that's a good closing spot for today. Do me a favor and pack up your belongings right now and let's form into a standing circle.
All right! In honor of Thanksgiving, I'd like to hear from ten different folks: one thing you're thankful for. Go.
The Circle of Power - a really fun way to mix things up during those final, finicky moments of class between now and the winter break.
